full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll tell you a bit about what we're doing to begin with. We're speaking to as many 2nd year eng, women engineering students as we can. We're mainly talking to people that are going on placement. Are you going on placement?

Subject:	Hopefully.

Interviewer:	Ok. We're looking at why women have decided to do engineering as a career and what their expectations of the work placement are. We're looking at women's first experiences of the engineering industry. And then we're going to interview people again when they're on placement as well to find out how their expectations differ from what it really is like.

Subject:	Its not actually engineering, its air transport management.

Interviewer:	Yes, that's ok, we've used a loose definition of engineering. Its mainly looking at engineering as a male dominated field, which is mainly why we've included your particular degree. But what we're hoping to do at the end of the 2 year project, is to put a report together and give it to the engineering councils and hopefully try and improve the situation for women in the industry. So to begin with I'm just going to ask you a few background questions about why you decided to do engineering and stuff like that. So its air transport management you're doing?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok, and what 'A' levels did you do?

Subject:	History, Geography and Computing.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Grammer school – female.

Interviewer:	Girl's school? Have you got any work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I did 6 months at a flying school (last week?)

Interviewer:	Oh excellent. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers or in the air transport industry?

Subject:	My Mum's a hairdresser.

Interviewer:	Ok, so when did you decide that you were interested in air transport?

Subject:	Well, being an RAF cadet, I was kind of looking for a degree course and I actually found it through my boyfriend at the time, who was doing it, and it was a bit different from what I was looking at – I was looking at something geography based. It kind of really grabbed my attention actually, 'cos I was looking at all the engineering stuff he was doing actually, like how planes are designed and things like that, it was really interesting.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider doing aeronautical engineering?

Subject:	No, I just, I'd rather do management, not really engineering.

Interviewer:	Ok, what other factors do you think influenced your decision? Were your family supportive?

Subject:	Yes they were actually, I want to join the RAF so an air related degree is quite useful for them. Yeah, no-one in my family's done anything like it. I've got a sister who's a lawyer, and my brother's a sailor.

Interviewer:	Did you have any careers advice or anything like that?

Subject:	Only from the RAF.

Interviewer:	Right, ok, so did you always know that you wanted to follow that sort of career?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are you hoping to carry on in the RAF?

Subject:	Yeah, I want to do flight management.

Interviewer:	Ok, so were they quite supportive in saying what degrees would be good?

Subject:	They think its quite useful, but they're not too bothered. But I think it will be quite useful if I came out the RAF, I can carry on doing what I like, so, its something I enjoy.

Interviewer:	You mentioned your boyfriend at the time, did you know anyone else that had done, did you have any other connections?

Subject:	Not really, I mean I met quite a few of his course mates, but I mean there's only a few courses run in the country so to find someone else who does it is quite difficult. But I spoke to him and I spoke to his course mates, so.

Interviewer:	Did you always know that you wanted to the sandwich course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok, and how did you decide to come to [this university]? Obviously you didn't have that much choice?

Subject:	No. I had a look at [university], that was my sister's old university – it just didn't appeal. It's in the middle of a city, and the tower blocks are horrible. And erm, just [this university's] a really nice campus and 'cos I'd been here quite a bit before I really liked it here. Its like where I come from at home, so.

Interviewer:	Did you realise that it was so male-dominated?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	No, 'cos everything I've done, like the RAF and the courses I've been on, I've been used to being the only girl there, so I'm quite used to it, it doesn't bother me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled into…

Subject:	Yes, definitely. Yes, 'cos coming from a girl's school, most of the kind of leaflets we seem to get are like politics and English, and you don't really get that many engineering ones. Whereas the boys school next to us, were always going on about being engineers and aeronautical, so there's a big difference between the girls and boys schools.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done at an early stage in education to encourage women?

Subject:	For engineering, I think probably do more open days. I know that they do them at [this university], erm, but at my local school there's not a lot advertised. It's not something that's really encouraged I don't think. It's not seen as a girl's kind of (?) to be honest.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	I don't know, I think its just kind of – I don't know why, its kind of maths and science and the boys always traditionally come from ones that do it, kind of stereotyping so.

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you think make a good air transport manager?

Subject:	Erm, to be rational, and er pretty well-informed of what you're doing and what you're managing. You need a lot of background knowledge, whatever, you've got to do consultancy or running the airport. Erm, that's about it really, it's just theory at the moment rather than actual hard knowledge, but.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things are more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	I have (a lecturer on my course that?) management qualities, they're more looked for in kind of, you know, in management. Some females aren't so good at that. But then obviously there are some females on the course that are quite good at getting the boys to do what we want.

Interviewer:	Well that was going to be one of my next questions. Do you think there are any advantages to being a woman in that sort of environment?

Subject:	Yes, its unusual. (lost words) Its always guys that come in to talk, we've got no female lecturers, so it's a bit unusual so maybe we can make our mark, you know, stand out, be a bit different. I'd like to see some more female lecturers.

Interviewer:	Well that was another point I was going to ask you, did you say you haven't got any female lecturers?

Subject:	I've got a female tutor, but I haven't seen her at all.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes, it would. It would be nice to see what they've done as well, 'cos we've got one lecturer who told us one of his experiences how the women were so lovely and their (French?) and all the men like them. What about us? Where are the (men?) for us? You know, it'd be nice to see a woman doing it, or coming in doing talks and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Is it kind of, if they can do it, so can I?

Subject:	Yes, because with the RAF stuff I've done, I'm normally the only girl, so I've got to prove myself really well, so you know, it'd be nice to see some more women.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you do have to work harder to prove yourself because you are a woman?

Subject:	Yes, especially with the boys. They always know all the stuff about the planes and all the technical bits, and if you're a female the (plane spotting's?) a bit (?). And you know it is, it is very stereotyped.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think there are any other disadvantages to being a woman?

Subject:	Not on my course really.

Interviewer:	Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yes, I think so. I knew it was going to be a management course. Erm, I expected it to be male-dominated. I probably expected a little bit more emphasis on aeronautical, planes and stuff, I'm quite surprised by er, we're doing a psychology module at the moment and marketing. You know, its like why do people want to travel? So I'm quite surprised by some of that. But I don't know really what I expected, that's pretty much it.

Interviewer:	What would you say have been the best and worse things about the course so far?

Subject:	Oh we've got this really cracking lecturer called [name], and he's been so enthusiastic, it's just like really good. I think it's the lecturers who make or break the course. We've got another one whose pretty boring. But yes, meeting everyone, you kind of get to know everyone and what they do. Most of the guys work in like the airports round here, so its cool to meet people who like what you do.

Interviewer:	What about the worse things?

Subject:	I can't really – I think – mmm, maybe the focus of the course. I think some people didn't actually expect it to be so management related because its in civil and building, they expected it more like, how a plane is built, because there's so much theory, they're a bit put off by it. But I think in the long run, its more helpful for a job.

Interviewer:	You said you've got a personal tutor, a female personal tutor, have you been to see her at all?

Subject:	No, I've seen her once. She's not actually anything to do with my course, which makes it hard. I'm not sure if she actually knows what my name is, she just calls me [shortened version of surname] (laughs). I normally go to the course tutor – if I've got a problem, he's really good about it.

Interviewer:	Ok so would you rather have someone more related to your course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Were you bothered whether your personal tutor is male or female?

Subject:	No, not for this course I don't think.

Interviewer:	Ok, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Probably my lecturers. Get, to motivate – it's pretty hard sometimes. Some of the lecturers, yes. If you like the lectures and the lecturer, you're more inclined, I think, to work. But if you just go along and you don't enjoy it, then you don't want to do anything really.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do much group work so far?

Subject:	Yes, we've, I think we've done one group work module per term. (lost words)

Interviewer:	How do you decide who you're going to work with when you do group work?

Subject:	One of them it was my housemate and my bestfriend, and the other one we got put into groups for.

Interviewer:	Do you find that men or women are better to work with or?

Subject:	I normally do work with, the guys are pretty organised, they know what they want you to do. Erm I think it's kind of equal, you know, you;ve all got to achieve the goal so you may as well get on and do it. Some of the guys can't be bothered, but others are like let's get it out the way, lets plan it. And my best friend's so laid back we leave it til the last night and get through it fine.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different qualities to group work?

Subject:	I think they do, but I think its down to the individuals, so probably not. I sort of said that they are because they know what they want to do, but if I've got to get a point across, if I think they're doing it wrong, then I'll let them know, if I think they need to be told what to do. But I can't say if its guys as a whole.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	No, everyone just gets on and does it. We've done really well, we've got like B's and A's so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work will help you in like a work environment?

Subject:	Yes because the whole like team work and its like using everyone's skills, 'cos when you all come together, we all know different bits and pieces, so you can do it like that. Erm, yes I find it easier to work as a group actually, than on my own. I enjoy it more, just talking to people and finding out what they know, and what they know, and getting it altogether.

Interviewer:	What bits of teaching and advice that you've had do you think will help you when you're on the placement?

Subject:	One of my lecturers who said when you get out to work forget everything you've been taught and start again (laughs). I think it's just a learning curve really, you know. I don't think I could take anything I've learnt just now and put it in the workplace, but it kind of gives you a view of transport overall, you know, where it's going. I do think that it'll be a steep learning curve when I go out to work.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any skills or anything that you will…

Subject:	Organisation, a bit of essay writing I think. Erm, apart from that, not a lot.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience? I've asked you that already…

Subject:	Yeas, I worked at an airport – well not at an airport, at a flying school doing work experience one day a week. I don't think it was particularly helpful. I didn't do a lot, but I saw how the company worked.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will take anything from that experience to the placement?

Subject:	Just to see how the workplace got on, the people were so relaxed, and you know, got on really well. They were more friends than colleagues. Erm, I think that's quite important when it's a very small company, so I think that worked well. I'd like to work for part of a small company rather than a kind of big one. I'd like to know everyone who works there.

Interviewer:	Do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement at like this point in time?

Subject:	Yes, it's just finding the placement to do it in. That's been the biggest problem for everyone on my course.

Interviewer:	Is that the type of course that you're doing?

Subject:	Yes and the problems with the aviation industry at the moment.

Interviewer:	Has anyone got a placement yet?

Subject:	Mmm, my best friend applied for one and she got one with [budget airline], but its baggage check-in (laughs), which isn't much to do with our course. You know, its stuff like that. A few of the guys have got jobs already, which I think they'll carry on. But it's getting one that's really relevant. I want to try erm, consultancy, but I don't know if there'd be any placements.

Interviewer:	Have you applied to anything like that?

Subject:	I've applied to [company] in [USA] I'm still waiting to hear on that one. I've applied to [company] in marketing and sales, and I applied to a company called [company] on Friday and then I found out that they've shed 540 jobs out of 600, so I don't think I'll be working there. But yes, most of the airlines, it's really difficult to get the placements. It's not what you know and how good you are, it's who you know and who can get you the placement.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that the educational experience and the way that you're taught will reflect what it's really like in industry?

Subject:	Yes, I think so because many of our lecturers do – have worked in the industry. They're always telling us about when they were doing this and that so they kind of, they try and show you how you can use what you're learning and help you…

Interviewer:	Give you real life examples?

Subject:	Yes. But I find a lot of them do research mainly. I think, you know, writing up papers about what's going on, so sometimes it's useful, sometimes it's not, but they generally have the idea about what's going on overall.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will help prepare you for the industry, or do you think they should be doing anything else to help prepare you for when you do go?

Subject:	Yes, I could do with a little bit more help. I feel that, I do feel a bit daunted by the placement year. I don't know what to expect. I don't know if I'm going to turn up and make a complete mess out of it (laughs).

Interviewer:	What do you think they could do to help that situation?

Subject:	Well, normally if we've got, you know, like with the placements, they do like a lecture, not really a lecture, but get us altogether and tell us what to expect. So maybe a few more sessions like that or talk to the course tutor, get hold of, you know, students who have done it before, and ask them what's going on. I've spoken to one of the students who did the Washington placement and asked them what to expect, and he was just like, office work really, sending out emails and stuff like that. But, I think there needs to be more. You know, we get these emails through saying there's a placement, apply for it, but you don't know what you're going to be doing. So it's a bit off putting.

Interviewer:	Ok, why do you think that you do want to go on placement?

Subject:	For the experience it will bring. I think that if I decide to go into the RAF, and then come out maybe in 6 or12 years, I can at least go back and say well I've worked doing this, I'm not just RAF, so can you take me on that. And plus, if things don't go well, it's still the experience, and it will (show?) what I don't want to do whether, whether I've enjoyed it or not.

Interviewer:	Could you have done a placement in the RAF at all?

Subject:	I tried. They only do placements for actual engineers, proper.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's maybe a good thing though, that you can't, because it means that if you do get a placement, you will have that other experience?

Subject:	Yes, my mum thinks it a bit make or break for the services, she thinks it's for a very particular kind of person. I actually applied for one with the army as well, Royal Logistics, but I decided not to because I don't think it's kind of the career I really want. I don't think I could do it for a year, but the RAF appeals more. 

Interviewer:	Has anyone really encouraged you or discouraged you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, one of our lectures has these little pep talks, which he says, you know, get it altogether otherwise you'll fail. Erm, he likes to encourage us but I don't think it works. Like, he did tell us that if you go on a placement you come back and you're more willing to work, you know, to achieve like a 2.1. And he said you know if you just go through the whole 3 years you get kind of a bit bored of it really, so that kind of encourages us (more than anything?)

Interviewer:	Do you think that once you've been on placement you'll use anything you've learnt on placement back in university?

Subject:	Hopefully, I, you know, it might provide me with my end of year project or something like that and then contacts to help me do it. So hopefully it will be useful.

Interviewer:	When you've been applying for placements what sort of things are you looking for in a company?

Subject:	Erm, probably aviation related, although I've applied to [company]. Erm I think it all depends on the company, whether it, you know, I have a look at its website and see what they do and see what interests me most. I think it'll be logistics, sales and marketing because I can do all those things from my degree, its pretty varied – consultancy, if I can find a placement there.

Interviewer:	So is the main thing you've been looking at the type of work that they do?

Subject:	Yes, and seeing what interests me most.

Interviewer:	After that have you looked at training opportunities and things like that, or salary or career prospects or anything like that?

Subject:	Yes. Erm, the training programme, I'd actually like to travel, so world-wide would be nice, so I've had a look at that. Erm, other than that, not really.

Interviewer:	Have you done much research into the companies that you've applied to?

Subject:	 [Company], I did a fair amount, my whole covering letter was based on the research. [company], I've had a look at, I don't find their website too helpful, but I spoke to the people at the careers service and [company] (live?) near the airport, so.

Interviewer:	Have the university been helpful in helping you find a placement, especially with your course being difficult for finding placements? Have you found them helpful or do you think they could do anything else?

Subject:	Careers don't tend to know that much about transport, but they give us a few places to kind of apply to. Our course lecturers try and tell us a couple of placements each week. One of my friends whose in, who does systems engineering, he said that his department have sent out his CV for him, he's like said what he wants (?) and they've sent it out to like 40 or 50 companies and then himself he sent out about 20. Our department are like, well this is what you've got to do, do it. So it's quite on us, but they kind of get us started.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be better to have more help then?

Subject:	Yes, 'cos on top of your coursework you've got to write the letters, you've got to find the placements. And its quite helpful for them to send us the things but when you get it through your email box its like oh here's a placement, apply for it if you want, and its like, later, I've got stuff to do, so I think we could do with a little bit more help.

Interviewer:	Did you have the option to be sponsored at all?

Subject:	Erm, I didn't personally no. But it was kind of open to me when I was to do the RAF, but I didn't want to go for it.

Interviewer:	Why did you decide not to do that?

Subject:	Just in case I decided while I was at university that I didn't want to go in the RAF, and it was a lot of money to pay back. So, I didn't want to make that mistake and then have it hanging over me, for 6 or however may years afterwards.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there would have been any advantages to doing it? Apart from the money?

Subject:	Erm, probably, because I would know what I was going to do for a career, that would be, you know, I wouldn't have to think about placements, and the university air squadron, that's the only thing, the only real advantages I think.

Interviewer:	Ok, what are you really expecting to get out of a placement? In terms of say skills and what you're going to learn?

Subject:	I think working in an office environment is going to be the biggest thing that, it's going to show me how to do it. Because, no experience I've done so far has been in an office, so I don't know what to expect, and you know, how people kind of work together. Team working and probably just getting used to working as part of a small team would be cool.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do you think will be the best and worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	I think it's the whole scared factor of what to do, it's such a, it's going to be such a new experience and such a different one from university. You're going out, you're working and you're earning your own money, whereas here you just turn up for a lecture if you feel like it. I think that's going to be the biggest shock.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will be a good thing or a bad thing though?

Subject:	I think it will be a mixture of both, you know, the (outcome?) generally and it will be something to learn pretty fast. So I think it's got its good and bad things, that'll – it will give you a bit of a shock on how to (deliver?) it properly.

Interviewer:	So it's quite scary but the final outcome will be…

Subject:	Yes, it'll be worth it in the end.

Interviewer:	How do you expect work to differ from university? You've said that it will be different, but like how you're treated and things like that?

Subject:	I think I'll probably be treated more like an adult. Because here they do treat you still like a bit of a student, still growing up. Erm, I'll have my own responsibilities. I don't think I'll have anyone chasing round after me saying don't forget to do this or that or you know, I think it'll probably make me grow up.

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	Hopefully in the RAF, somewhere in Britain or around the world, managing planes.

Interviewer:	What about in 10 years time? 

Subject:	Probably still in the RAF. I'm hoping to do it as a long-term career but, it all depends really.

Interviewer:	Is that your ideal career then?

Subject:	Yes. I'd like to do a bit of management consultancy afterwards, but yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you'll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve that?

Subject:	Yes, there'll be interviews and all the testing you have to go through. But I figure I've gone through it once and got through that, but doing it agains, sort of, erm. Yes, I think the whole change of lifestyle again is different from university so..

Interviewer:	Do you think that your experiences so far will help you with the application process?

Subject:	Yes I think so, erm. I'm getting used to writing my CV and knowing what to say, and putting my thoughts across, and you know, managing people which is quite an essential skill for it I think. 

Interviewer:	Ok, you've said that you'd like to travel, do you want to do that long term or?

Subject:	Erm, I'm not sure. I think its more kind of while I'm younger, I'd like to see the world before I've got too many responsibilities.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the career prospects are good in what you're doing?

Subject:	Yes, I think that for my course, you can do so much with it. Erm, there isn't just one thing that I can do either. I can manage, do logistics, supply chain management, sales and marketing. There's just so much I could do with it.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	No, I'm happy. I can't see myself doing anything else.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the culture and characteristics of air transport management?

Subject:	Oh gosh, male dominated, management, planes and lots of writing.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that it is so male dominated?

Subject:	Planes, boys and their toys. You know, you don't really find many women who are interested in planes I don't think. I don't know why.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	I do wonder about that, I do sometimes think that the boys bring it up in debate. You know, if you're going to choose a woman over a man. I think I'll probably have to wait and see. But it does cross my mind.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you're educational experiences differ from other students like in social sciences or business or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, well business studies does help a lot on our course, and economics, so I'm probably at a disadvantage compared to some of them, but there's so many different 'A' levels coming into this, there's nothing really specific. I mean geography helps and computing, and its all just brought in and so the first year was all just bringing us up to standard, but I think economics helps the most.

Interviewer:	Ok that's everything that I had to ask you really. Yes, thank you very much.

turns.text: Ok, so were they quite supportive in saying what degrees would be good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They think its quite useful, but they're not too bothered. But I think it will be quite useful if I came out the RAF, I can carry on doing what I like, so, its something I enjoy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned your boyfriend at the time, did you know anyone else that had done, did you have any other connections?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, I mean I met quite a few of his course mates, but I mean there's only a few courses run in the country so to find someone else who does it is quite difficult. But I spoke to him and I spoke to his course mates, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you always know that you wanted to the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, and how did you decide to come to [this university]? Obviously you didn't have that much choice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I had a look at [university], that was my sister's old university – it just didn't appeal. It's in the middle of a city, and the tower blocks are horrible. And erm, just [this university's] a really nice campus and 'cos I'd been here quite a bit before I really liked it here. Its like where I come from at home, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you realise that it was so male-dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, 'cos everything I've done, like the RAF and the courses I've been on, I've been used to being the only girl there, so I'm quite used to it, it doesn't bother me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled into…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely. Yes, 'cos coming from a girl's school, most of the kind of leaflets we seem to get are like politics and English, and you don't really get that many engineering ones. Whereas the boys school next to us, were always going on about being engineers and aeronautical, so there's a big difference between the girls and boys schools.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done at an early stage in education to encourage women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: For engineering, I think probably do more open days. I know that they do them at [this university], erm, but at my local school there's not a lot advertised. It's not something that's really encouraged I don't think. It's not seen as a girl's kind of (?) to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know, I think its just kind of – I don't know why, its kind of maths and science and the boys always traditionally come from ones that do it, kind of stereotyping so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics do you think make a good air transport manager?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, to be rational, and er pretty well-informed of what you're doing and what you're managing. You need a lot of background knowledge, whatever, you've got to do consultancy or running the airport. Erm, that's about it really, it's just theory at the moment rather than actual hard knowledge, but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things are more male or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have (a lecturer on my course that?) management qualities, they're more looked for in kind of, you know, in management. Some females aren't so good at that. But then obviously there are some females on the course that are quite good at getting the boys to do what we want.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well that was going to be one of my next questions. Do you think there are any advantages to being a woman in that sort of environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, its unusual. (lost words) Its always guys that come in to talk, we've got no female lecturers, so it's a bit unusual so maybe we can make our mark, you know, stand out, be a bit different. I'd like to see some more female lecturers.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well that was another point I was going to ask you, did you say you haven't got any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I've got a female tutor, but I haven't seen her at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it would. It would be nice to see what they've done as well, 'cos we've got one lecturer who told us one of his experiences how the women were so lovely and their (French?) and all the men like them. What about us? Where are the (men?) for us? You know, it'd be nice to see a woman doing it, or coming in doing talks and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it kind of, if they can do it, so can I?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, because with the RAF stuff I've done, I'm normally the only girl, so I've got to prove myself really well, so you know, it'd be nice to see some more women.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you do have to work harder to prove yourself because you are a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, especially with the boys. They always know all the stuff about the planes and all the technical bits, and if you're a female the (plane spotting's?) a bit (?). And you know it is, it is very stereotyped.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think there are any other disadvantages to being a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not on my course really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think so. I knew it was going to be a management course. Erm, I expected it to be male-dominated. I probably expected a little bit more emphasis on aeronautical, planes and stuff, I'm quite surprised by er, we're doing a psychology module at the moment and marketing. You know, its like why do people want to travel? So I'm quite surprised by some of that. But I don't know really what I expected, that's pretty much it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say have been the best and worse things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh we've got this really cracking lecturer called [name], and he's been so enthusiastic, it's just like really good. I think it's the lecturers who make or break the course. We've got another one whose pretty boring. But yes, meeting everyone, you kind of get to know everyone and what they do. Most of the guys work in like the airports round here, so its cool to meet people who like what you do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the worse things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can't really – I think – mmm, maybe the focus of the course. I think some people didn't actually expect it to be so management related because its in civil and building, they expected it more like, how a plane is built, because there's so much theory, they're a bit put off by it. But I think in the long run, its more helpful for a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said you've got a personal tutor, a female personal tutor, have you been to see her at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I've seen her once. She's not actually anything to do with my course, which makes it hard. I'm not sure if she actually knows what my name is, she just calls me [shortened version of surname] (laughs). I normally go to the course tutor – if I've got a problem, he's really good about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok so would you rather have someone more related to your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you bothered whether your personal tutor is male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not for this course I don't think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably my lecturers. Get, to motivate – it's pretty hard sometimes. Some of the lecturers, yes. If you like the lectures and the lecturer, you're more inclined, I think, to work. But if you just go along and you don't enjoy it, then you don't want to do anything really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do much group work so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, we've, I think we've done one group work module per term. (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide who you're going to work with when you do group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One of them it was my housemate and my bestfriend, and the other one we got put into groups for.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that men or women are better to work with or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I normally do work with, the guys are pretty organised, they know what they want you to do. Erm I think it's kind of equal, you know, you;ve all got to achieve the goal so you may as well get on and do it. Some of the guys can't be bothered, but others are like let's get it out the way, lets plan it. And my best friend's so laid back we leave it til the last night and get through it fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different qualities to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they do, but I think its down to the individuals, so probably not. I sort of said that they are because they know what they want to do, but if I've got to get a point across, if I think they're doing it wrong, then I'll let them know, if I think they need to be told what to do. But I can't say if its guys as a whole.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, everyone just gets on and does it. We've done really well, we've got like B's and A's so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the group work will help you in like a work environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes because the whole like team work and its like using everyone's skills, 'cos when you all come together, we all know different bits and pieces, so you can do it like that. Erm, yes I find it easier to work as a group actually, than on my own. I enjoy it more, just talking to people and finding out what they know, and what they know, and getting it altogether.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What bits of teaching and advice that you've had do you think will help you when you're on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One of my lecturers who said when you get out to work forget everything you've been taught and start again (laughs). I think it's just a learning curve really, you know. I don't think I could take anything I've learnt just now and put it in the workplace, but it kind of gives you a view of transport overall, you know, where it's going. I do think that it'll be a steep learning curve when I go out to work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any skills or anything that you will…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Organisation, a bit of essay writing I think. Erm, apart from that, not a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience? I've asked you that already…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeas, I worked at an airport – well not at an airport, at a flying school doing work experience one day a week. I don't think it was particularly helpful. I didn't do a lot, but I saw how the company worked.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will take anything from that experience to the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just to see how the workplace got on, the people were so relaxed, and you know, got on really well. They were more friends than colleagues. Erm, I think that's quite important when it's a very small company, so I think that worked well. I'd like to work for part of a small company rather than a kind of big one. I'd like to know everyone who works there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel ready and prepared to go on placement at like this point in time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it's just finding the placement to do it in. That's been the biggest problem for everyone on my course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that the type of course that you're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and the problems with the aviation industry at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has anyone got a placement yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mmm, my best friend applied for one and she got one with [budget airline], but its baggage check-in (laughs), which isn't much to do with our course. You know, its stuff like that. A few of the guys have got jobs already, which I think they'll carry on. But it's getting one that's really relevant. I want to try erm, consultancy, but I don't know if there'd be any placements.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you applied to anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I've applied to [company] in [USA] I'm still waiting to hear on that one. I've applied to [company] in marketing and sales, and I applied to a company called [company] on Friday and then I found out that they've shed 540 jobs out of 600, so I don't think I'll be working there. But yes, most of the airlines, it's really difficult to get the placements. It's not what you know and how good you are, it's who you know and who can get you the placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that the educational experience and the way that you're taught will reflect what it's really like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think so because many of our lecturers do – have worked in the industry. They're always telling us about when they were doing this and that so they kind of, they try and show you how you can use what you're learning and help you…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Give you real life examples?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. But I find a lot of them do research mainly. I think, you know, writing up papers about what's going on, so sometimes it's useful, sometimes it's not, but they generally have the idea about what's going on overall.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that will help prepare you for the industry, or do you think they should be doing anything else to help prepare you for when you do go?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I could do with a little bit more help. I feel that, I do feel a bit daunted by the placement year. I don't know what to expect. I don't know if I'm going to turn up and make a complete mess out of it (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think they could do to help that situation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, normally if we've got, you know, like with the placements, they do like a lecture, not really a lecture, but get us altogether and tell us what to expect. So maybe a few more sessions like that or talk to the course tutor, get hold of, you know, students who have done it before, and ask them what's going on. I've spoken to one of the students who did the Washington placement and asked them what to expect, and he was just like, office work really, sending out emails and stuff like that. But, I think there needs to be more. You know, we get these emails through saying there's a placement, apply for it, but you don't know what you're going to be doing. So it's a bit off putting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, why do you think that you do want to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: For the experience it will bring. I think that if I decide to go into the RAF, and then come out maybe in 6 or12 years, I can at least go back and say well I've worked doing this, I'm not just RAF, so can you take me on that. And plus, if things don't go well, it's still the experience, and it will (show?) what I don't want to do whether, whether I've enjoyed it or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Could you have done a placement in the RAF at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I tried. They only do placements for actual engineers, proper.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's maybe a good thing though, that you can't, because it means that if you do get a placement, you will have that other experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, my mum thinks it a bit make or break for the services, she thinks it's for a very particular kind of person. I actually applied for one with the army as well, Royal Logistics, but I decided not to because I don't think it's kind of the career I really want. I don't think I could do it for a year, but the RAF appeals more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has anyone really encouraged you or discouraged you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, one of our lectures has these little pep talks, which he says, you know, get it altogether otherwise you'll fail. Erm, he likes to encourage us but I don't think it works. Like, he did tell us that if you go on a placement you come back and you're more willing to work, you know, to achieve like a 2.1. And he said you know if you just go through the whole 3 years you get kind of a bit bored of it really, so that kind of encourages us (more than anything?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that once you've been on placement you'll use anything you've learnt on placement back in university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, I, you know, it might provide me with my end of year project or something like that and then contacts to help me do it. So hopefully it will be useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you've been applying for placements what sort of things are you looking for in a company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably aviation related, although I've applied to [company]. Erm I think it all depends on the company, whether it, you know, I have a look at its website and see what they do and see what interests me most. I think it'll be logistics, sales and marketing because I can do all those things from my degree, its pretty varied – consultancy, if I can find a placement there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So is the main thing you've been looking at the type of work that they do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and seeing what interests me most.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: After that have you looked at training opportunities and things like that, or salary or career prospects or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Erm, the training programme, I'd actually like to travel, so world-wide would be nice, so I've had a look at that. Erm, other than that, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you done much research into the companies that you've applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company], I did a fair amount, my whole covering letter was based on the research. [company], I've had a look at, I don't find their website too helpful, but I spoke to the people at the careers service and [company] (live?) near the airport, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have the university been helpful in helping you find a placement, especially with your course being difficult for finding placements? Have you found them helpful or do you think they could do anything else?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Careers don't tend to know that much about transport, but they give us a few places to kind of apply to. Our course lecturers try and tell us a couple of placements each week. One of my friends whose in, who does systems engineering, he said that his department have sent out his CV for him, he's like said what he wants (?) and they've sent it out to like 40 or 50 companies and then himself he sent out about 20. Our department are like, well this is what you've got to do, do it. So it's quite on us, but they kind of get us started.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be better to have more help then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, 'cos on top of your coursework you've got to write the letters, you've got to find the placements. And its quite helpful for them to send us the things but when you get it through your email box its like oh here's a placement, apply for it if you want, and its like, later, I've got stuff to do, so I think we could do with a little bit more help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have the option to be sponsored at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn't personally no. But it was kind of open to me when I was to do the RAF, but I didn't want to go for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you decide not to do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just in case I decided while I was at university that I didn't want to go in the RAF, and it was a lot of money to pay back. So, I didn't want to make that mistake and then have it hanging over me, for 6 or however may years afterwards.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there would have been any advantages to doing it? Apart from the money?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably, because I would know what I was going to do for a career, that would be, you know, I wouldn't have to think about placements, and the university air squadron, that's the only thing, the only real advantages I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what are you really expecting to get out of a placement? In terms of say skills and what you're going to learn?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think working in an office environment is going to be the biggest thing that, it's going to show me how to do it. Because, no experience I've done so far has been in an office, so I don't know what to expect, and you know, how people kind of work together. Team working and probably just getting used to working as part of a small team would be cool.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do you think will be the best and worst things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's the whole scared factor of what to do, it's such a, it's going to be such a new experience and such a different one from university. You're going out, you're working and you're earning your own money, whereas here you just turn up for a lecture if you feel like it. I think that's going to be the biggest shock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that will be a good thing or a bad thing though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will be a mixture of both, you know, the (outcome?) generally and it will be something to learn pretty fast. So I think it's got its good and bad things, that'll – it will give you a bit of a shock on how to (deliver?) it properly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it's quite scary but the final outcome will be…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it'll be worth it in the end.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you expect work to differ from university? You've said that it will be different, but like how you're treated and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I'll probably be treated more like an adult. Because here they do treat you still like a bit of a student, still growing up. Erm, I'll have my own responsibilities. I don't think I'll have anyone chasing round after me saying don't forget to do this or that or you know, I think it'll probably make me grow up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully in the RAF, somewhere in Britain or around the world, managing planes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably still in the RAF. I'm hoping to do it as a long-term career but, it all depends really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I'd like to do a bit of management consultancy afterwards, but yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you'll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, there'll be interviews and all the testing you have to go through. But I figure I've gone through it once and got through that, but doing it agains, sort of, erm. Yes, I think the whole change of lifestyle again is different from university so..

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your experiences so far will help you with the application process?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I think so, erm. I'm getting used to writing my CV and knowing what to say, and putting my thoughts across, and you know, managing people which is quite an essential skill for it I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, you've said that you'd like to travel, do you want to do that long term or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm not sure. I think its more kind of while I'm younger, I'd like to see the world before I've got too many responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the career prospects are good in what you're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think that for my course, you can do so much with it. Erm, there isn't just one thing that I can do either. I can manage, do logistics, supply chain management, sales and marketing. There's just so much I could do with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I'm happy. I can't see myself doing anything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the culture and characteristics of air transport management?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh gosh, male dominated, management, planes and lots of writing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Planes, boys and their toys. You know, you don't really find many women who are interested in planes I don't think. I don't know why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that it is so male dominated will cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do wonder about that, I do sometimes think that the boys bring it up in debate. You know, if you're going to choose a woman over a man. I think I'll probably have to wait and see. But it does cross my mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you're educational experiences differ from other students like in social sciences or business or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well business studies does help a lot on our course, and economics, so I'm probably at a disadvantage compared to some of them, but there's so many different 'A' levels coming into this, there's nothing really specific. I mean geography helps and computing, and its all just brought in and so the first year was all just bringing us up to standard, but I think economics helps the most.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that's everything that I had to ask you really. Yes, thank you very much.
